# Association {#sec-association}

[Learning what is bad]{.lb-subtitle}

<div data-life="status" data-stage="1.5"></div>

::: {.lb-takeaway}
**New:** the first learning within a life. After a bite that hurts, the look of what was bitten comes to mean
*bad*.

**Result:** in a world where every food is new, the animals learn which ones are poison and live about twice as
long as animals that cannot learn. Without the learning they lose more than half their fitness.
:::

Until now everything the animal knows was put there by evolution. That works for poison that looks the same in
every generation, but not for food that is new. In this stage all food is new: every kind of berry gets a new
colour in every life, and which kinds are poison is drawn anew.

<div data-life="brain" data-stage="1.5"></div>

## The circuit

One new cell, and one change to existing synapses:

- **`us_pain`**, the *teacher*, is driven by pain alone. When it fires, it sends a teaching signal. (*US* stands
  for *unconditioned stimulus*: something that matters without any learning, as pain does.)
- **The synapses from the look onto the *bad* cells** (`valence_av`) can now change during a life. A synapse grows
  when its input was just active and the teacher fires. These are the purple arrows in the diagram.

Nothing else has to change. The *bad* cells already turn the animal away and block the bite, so once the look of a
berry excites them, the animal treats that berry like the poison it was born knowing.

### What gets the blame

A bite hurts, and something has to take the blame. Getting this right was most of the work of this stage:

- **The lesson is about what sets the food apart.** If pain strengthened the whole look, one bad red berry would
  make the animal wary of every berry. Here the adapting eyes of the previous stage pay a second time: what all
  bushes share cancels out before it reaches a synapse, and what is left to take the blame is the colour.
- **The pain is brief.** When pain lasted several ticks, the teacher was still firing after the animal had turned
  to the next bush, and it learned to distrust the neighbour as much as the poison.
- **Every learnable synapse exists.** A synapse that is not there cannot learn, so all of them are present, the new
  ones starting at zero.

## Watching it work

One animal from the last generation, at two moments of its life. First, its first bite of a kind that is poison in
this life. Before the bite the *bad* cells are silent and `grasp` fires. One tick later the pain arrives, the
teacher fires, and the *bad* cells and `no_feed` switch on by reflex, as before this stage. What cannot be seen is
the change the teacher leaves in the synapses.

<div data-life="strip" data-stage="1.5" data-example="first_lesson"></div>

Later in the same life the animal comes up to a bush of the same kind. **Nothing hurts now, and yet the *bad* cells
fire and `no_feed` holds the bite back.** The animal moves on. It learned this; no ancestor could have told it.

<div data-life="strip" data-stage="1.5" data-example="lesson_again"></div>

## Biology

A sea slug that is shocked after a touch learns to pull back from the touch. A rat that gets sick after a new food
avoids that food afterwards. This is *associative learning*: something neutral (the touch, the taste) comes to
predict something that matters (the shock, the sickness), and the animal responds to the first as it would to the
second.

At the level of synapses, worked out in the sea slug *Aplysia* and the fruit fly, it has three parts. A sensory
neuron that was just active leaves a short trace at its synapses. A teaching signal, released when something bad
happens, reaches many synapses at once. Only the synapses with a fresh trace are strengthened. The circuit above
is this picture in its simplest form.

## The world

Four kinds of berry bush, all new in every life: each life draws a new colour for every kind, and which two of the
four are poison. The bushes still look like berry bushes; a new kind differs from the others in colour, the way a
new berry is still recognisably a berry.

Half of all bushes are poison, so an animal that cannot learn pays on every second bush it tries, all its life.
Leaving everything unknown alone is not an option either: there is nothing else to eat.

<div data-life="settings" data-stage="1.5"></div>

## Did it work?

<div data-life="verdict" data-stage="1.5" data-used="us_pain,no_plasticity"></div>

**Learning carries this stage.** Silence the teacher, or freeze every synapse at its inherited strength, and the
animals keep less than half their fitness. The old brain feels pain and turns away from it, but cannot change, so
it pays for every poison bush it tries, every time.

The learners still lead short lives: half of what they try is poison until they have learned it, and nothing yet
tells an animal that it is getting hungry.

*Learning switched off* freezes every synapse at its inherited strength; `us_pain` silences the teacher.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="What did not work: unlearning by tasting again"}
An earlier design had a second cell that lowered the aversion whenever something distrusted turned out to taste
fine. It worked when meals were fed to the brain in a test. In a living animal it never fired: aversion blocks the
bite, so food that is distrusted is never tasted again, and the mistake is never found out. That is why the lesson
has to land on the right food in the first place.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="What did not work: a world where learning was hardly worth it"}
The first versions of this world kept a familiar, safe kind of berry as half of all bushes. An animal that learned
nothing got by very well, and a perfect learner would have gained less than a tenth of its food. With so little to
win, evolution switched learning off whenever a lesson had any side effect. Removing the familiar food turned
this around.
:::
